Robotic Surgery

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Hailed as the future of patient care - robotic surgery is changing the face of the surgical landscape and SA is a part of this exciting technological development

Summary:
The da Vinci robotic system is a laparoscopic surgical tool used for urological procedures and radical prostatectomies. It has mechanical arms and wrists that twist and turn to mimic the movements of a surgeon's hands into smaller more precise movements. It also allows a surgeon to see the inside of a patient at a 10x magnification, making even the smallest veins and arteries visible. The machine is at the forefront of the battle against prostate cancer and brings a number of benefits to the patient.

Further information:
Pretoria's urological hospital has done more than 500 procedures with the machine, and their surgeon Dr LAnce Coetzee is SA's leading robotic surgeon. They have given us permission to film a procedure. We will also be speaking to case studies who have undergone the surgery. The robot also has camera's attached and we can use the footage.

Press Release:


Robotic Prostate Surgery
Hailed as the future of patient care, robotic technology is changing the face of prostate cancer surgery. The Da Vinci robotic system is a laparoscopic surgical tool used for urological procedures and radical prostatectomies. Its mechanical arms and wrists twist and turn to mimic the movements of a surgeon's hands allowing for infinitely smaller, more precise surgical work on even the smallest veins and arteries. Carte Blanche meets Dr Lance Coetzee, South Africa’s leading robotic surgeon.


Script:


Robotic Surgery

Voice
For most men it’s a very real fear – a routine visit to the doctor, a simple blood test and then a diagnosis that could equate to a death sentence… Prostate Cancer.

Sound Up Milton
Claire: When you heard the news, what was your initial reaction?

Milton: You know, fear. Fear… So it’s concern you know, very definitely a case of fear. No doubt about it.

Voice
Milton Espley-Jones is a successful businessman who was diagnosed with prostate problems earlier this year. Except for the obvious risk of death from the disease, Milton, like many men, also feared post-operative complications from the disease such as incontinence and impotence.

Sound Up Milton
In actual fact one; it’s worse than you think, and two; it would be a lie to sit down and say you wouldn’t miss all the male functions that one had if it weren’t that bad.

Voice
But some surgeons are now using innovative technologies in the fight against prostate cancer – and the results speak for themselves. Welcome to the age of robotics.

Link Claire
It may sound like science fiction, but robotic surgery is a reality and is happening right here in South Africa. It seems like a foreign concept but it will definitely change the way we think about surgical procedures in the future.

Sound Up Lance
We often speak about robot assisted laparoscopic surgery. So the concept is the same where it’s minimally invasive, we’ve done away with big incisions, reduced recovery times and at the same time improved the vision that you have and the accessibility to a lot of organs.

Voice
Doctor Lance Coetzee, from the Pretoria Urology Hospital, is one of South Africa’s leading robotic surgeons. He says the hospital has completed nearly 600 successful robotic prostatectomies – the surgical removal of all or part of the prostate gland. The operation is done for either benign conditions that cause urinary retention as well as for prostate cancer and other cancers of the bowel.

Sound Up Lance
The main procedures have been radical prostatectomies for prostate cancer, but we’ve also done two cystectomies for bladder cancer, and we are now getting going with kidney cancer and doing what we call partial nephrectomies or kidney sparing surgery, where instead of removing a whole kidney that may have a small tumor on the inferior pole of the kidney, we can now just remove the tumor and preserve a large part of the kidney.

Sound Up Norman
Well I came to Dr Coetzee’s consultation room and he said my Norman, I’m sorry to tell you that you’ve got cancer in your prostate. But, we can still take it out.

Voice
Norman Nzama was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2014. Although he was initially skeptical of robotic surgery he says the benefits eventually swayed his decision. And he admits his curiosity got the better of him.

Sound Up Norman
Me, I’m a curious man, very much curious, I wanted to see this robot, face to face with it.

Voice
Our cameras spent a day in theatre with Dr Coetzee to see the da Vinci surgical robot in action. The procedure starts with the anesthetized patient being connected to the robotic arms via hollow surgical tubes known as ports. The ports allow the robotic arms entry into the abdomen.

Sound Up Lance
The difference between robotic surgery and laparoscopic surgery is that with robotic surgery you have 560 degrees of wrist movement so you can get into small spaces especially in the bony pelvis, which you can’t do with laparoscopic surgery.

Voice
Once the robotic arms are in place, the surgery can begin, with the robot mimicking doctor Coetzee’s hand movements at the control panel.

Sound Up Lance
The robot eventually becomes an extension of your own hands. So it’s not like laparoscopic surgery where you’re operating with long instruments where you feel like you can’t move.

Voice
While the robotic arms follow the surgeons arm movements, the endo-wrist instruments are controlled by the fingers.

Sound Up Lance
Claire: So for you what was it like moving from open surgery to using this technology – from being tactile with your hands to eventually being intimate with a machine?

Lance: Well it is an adjustment obviously, and all of that depends on the training and depends on the volume of surgery you’re doing. The transition for a high volume open surgeon is actually very quick, because you know where the tissue planes are, you know the procedure, all you have to do is get used to is using a new instrument and a different way of doing it.

Voice
The robotic arms can cauterize blood vessels, add stitches and move into places where a surgeons hands never could. Another major advantage is the high-resolution cameras, which offer the surgeon a 10 x magnified view of the area being operated on.

Sound Up Lance
So in open surgery, especially when you’re working deep down in the pelvis you can’t actually see underneath the pubic bone or around certain corners. Whereas with the robot you can actually zoom in and get to all those areas and that is why the results and the outcomes are that much better.

Voice
There are literally thousands of nerve endings surrounding the prostate gland, so the better a surgeon is able to see and the more accurately the surgery can be performed, the better the chances of a successful procedure.

Sound Up Lance
Claire: And in terms of success rate, how has it performed?

Lance: The difference has been quite marked, in terms of recovery times, in terms of regaining function such as potency, urine control and getting the patients bck to work.

Sound Up Milton
Certainly they did say you could be in hospital for up to two weeks, as much as two weeks if you went the other route. Where this literally is less than a week, and that made a lot of sense to me.

Voice
Milton opted for robotic surgery after doing a lot of research into the subject and being impressed with the precision the robot offered.

Sound Up Milton
It literally can be controlled I gather up to about a millimeter, even less than a millimeter in terms of the cutting it does.

Voice
The robots’ arms certainly are dexterous, and in the hands of the right surgeon it can quite easily peel a grape without doing any damage to the fruit.

Sound Up Lance
The robot is only an instrument in the hands of the surgeon, and the robot doesn’t make a bad surgeon a good surgeon. You have to go through intensive training.

Voice
The training includes simulator training, mock operations and eventually surgeries performed under the supervision of experienced robotic surgeons.

Sound Up Milton
Claire: So when did you have the op?
Milton: Last night at 16:00.
Claire: So it’s almost 24 hours later and how are you feeling?
Milton: Fine, fine.

Voice
While the treatment certainly seems effective, a da Vinci robot will set a hospital back a cool R20 million rand. Costly consumables and maintenance end up meaning it’s a pricey exercise.

Sound Up Lance
Claire: You’re painting a pretty picture, so are there any challenges when it comes to robotic surgery here in South Africa?

Lance: I think the challenges will always be cost and accessibility to the machines, we’d like obviously to make this available to as many people as possible because we really believe in the technology and the outcomes.

Link Claire
It’s all well and good that this state of the art technology is here, but at such a high cost, will it benefit the man on the street?

Sound Up Shingai
Even if you look at the American data, it still has a premium cost probably about 30% more than any other type of simple radical prostatectomy. But then you have to balance that with all the other benefits that you get from using the robot.

Voice
Professor Shingai Mutambirwa heads the department of urology at the university of Limpopo.

Sound Up Shingai
we have other challenges at the moment, particularly primary health care, we still have a lot of basic things that still need to be addressed.

Voice
So for now, if you don’t have a medical aid that is willing to cover the procedure, you’ll end up footing the R200 000 bill. We spoke to Norman 48 hours after his robotic prostatectomy, where his recovery was going so well he was scheduled to leave the hospital the very next day.

Sound Up Norman
Claire: So you had your procedure two days ago?

Norman: Two days ago.

Claire: And how are you feeling?

Norman: No I’m alright, I’m alright.

Claire: Did they say everything went well?

Norman: It went well, the doctor said everything is fine.

Claire: And when will you be discharged?

Norman: Tomorrow.

Voice
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer for black men in South Africa and the second most common cancer among white men. Both surgeons and survivors agree that prevention is definitely better than cure.

Sound Up Milton
Well the first thing I would say, to anyone who thinks they have prostate cancer is go and check it out soon. Don’t wait a day. Don’t wait a day.

Sound Up Shingai
I think our priority is still to deal with the basics, preventative medicine, most of our prostate cancers are coming in when they can’t even be helped by a robot, they’ve already spread to other parts of the body.

Voice
Luckily for men who do suffer from the disease, technologies like robotic surgery are here to stay.

Sound Up Shingai
It is going to be the future, whether we like it or not, whether it’s going to be a cost issue or whether it’s training it is the way of the future. The aesthetic value of not having big scars, the decreased amount of blood loss, the faster recuperation for the patients is going to make people want to get robotic surgery done more and more.


PROMOS

PROMO 1 (15 sec)
Voice
Would you let a robot operate on you? We find out why so many men are more then happy to undergo robotic surgery.

Promo 2 (15 sec)
Voice
We take you inside the operating theatre where robotic surgery is at the forefront of the battle against prostate cancer.

Promo 3 (10sec)
It may sound like science fiction, but robotic surgery is not only a reality, it’s happening right here in South Africa. We take you inside the operating theatre.
